segments.text: Point to ْ, ّ, ً: “no vowel”, “double”, “-an”.

This is the letter people think of when they think "Arabic." ع (ʿayn) writes a sound made deep in the throat — one English simply does not have. And its history holds the best surprise in the whole alphabet: this consonant is the ancestor of our vowel O.
Break it apart — an open curve, then a bowl:
the open-mouth curve on top — like a small c opening to the left.
the bowl below, when ʿayn stands alone or ends a word — a scoop underneath.
Joined in the middle of a word it flattens into a little wedge; standing alone it shows the full curve-over-bowl. It is a connector, so it changes coat by position like sīn and lām.

You know the bowl family (ب/ن/ت/ث) from Lesson 4 and the hook-and-tail family (ح/خ/ج) from Lesson 7. ʿayn opens a third: its skeleton is shared with غ (ghayn), which is the same shape plus one dot above. Same trick, third time — by now you should expect it.

blocks.title: Script — The surprise: ʿayn becomes O

segments.text: ʿayn comes from Phoenician ʿayin, meaning "eye" — and the oldest forms were drawn as one. When the Greeks borrowed the Phoenician alphabet, they had no throat-sound like ʿ. So they did what borrowers do with a sign they can't use: they repurposed it — and turned the eye-shaped letter into the vowel omicron, our O.

So the round O you write is a Phoenician eye, and Arabic's ʿayn is the same sign that kept its original consonant job. (Compare the thread so far: ʾālep becomes A, bēt becomes B, mem becomes M, kaph becomes K, rēsh becomes R — and now ʿayin becomes O.)

You have been saying this sound since Chapter 1: السلام عليكم (as-salāmu ʿalaykum) — the ʿ in ʿalaykum is this letter. And the farewell you'll write two lessons from now, مع السلامة (as-salāma) (maʿa s-salāma), opens with it.

notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — ه (hāʾ) — the loop that never looks the same, Script — ة (tāʾ marbūṭa) — the "tied tāʾ" and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Two related shapes. ه (hāʾ) is a plain "h" — and the most shape-shifting letter you've met, wearing four genuinely different coats. Then ة, a letter built out of it, whose whole job is to say one grammatical thing: this word is feminine.

blocks.title: Script — ه (hāʾ) — the loop that never looks the same

segments.text: Break it apart — there is really just one piece:
the loop — a closed round body.

But that loop changes shape a lot by position more than any letter so far: standing alone it's a neat circle-ish loop; at the start it opens out; in the middle it becomes a small figure-of-eight pinched in the centre; at the end it trails. Same letter, four faces — the four-coats rule from Lesson 2 taken to its extreme.
From Phoenician hē — the ancestor of Greek epsilon and Latin E. (Another one for the family tree: ʾālep becomes A, bēt becomes B, hē becomes E, mem becomes M, ʿayin becomes O.)
Now look carefully at this:
ه = hāʾ's loop, no dots.
ة = the same loop + tāʾ's two dots above.

Its name says exactly what it is: tāʾ marbūṭa, "the tied-up tāʾ" — a ت (tāʾ, Lesson 4) whose ends have been tied into a loop. It appears only at the end of a word, and it is the standard mark of a feminine noun or adjective.

You already know its partner: back in Lesson 4 you learned ت with two dots above. Put those same two dots on a hāʾ loop and you get the feminine ending. Nothing new to memorise — just two known pieces combined.
Where you've seen it: the farewell مع السلامة (as-salāma) (maʿa s-salāma) ends in ة — salāma is feminine. That's the next lesson.

segments.text: The closing move. مع السلامة (as-salāma) (maʿa s-salāma) is how Arabic says goodbye — literally "with safety," go in peace. And the heart of it is a word you wrote all the way back in Lesson 3: سلام. Everything since has been leading here.
Two letters, both known:
م (mīm, Lesson 3) — round head, joining left into…
ع (ʿayn, Lesson 10) — the open curve over its bowl, closing the word.
becomes مع = maʿa, "with."
Look at what this is made of:
ال — the al- ("the"), alif + lām, both from Lessons 1–2. You've read it since Chapter 1 in الخير and السلام عليكم.
سلام — the exact word you assembled in Lesson 3: sīn, lām, alif, mīm.
ة — the tāʾ marbūṭa from Lesson 11, marking salāma as feminine.
So السلامة (as-salāma) = al- + salām + -a. You are not learning a new word; you are adding two edges to one you already own.

blocks.title: Script — The root s-l-m, one more time

segments.text: salām, salāma, islām, muslim — all from the Semitic root s–l–m, "peace, safety, wholeness." The greeting you learned first (السلام عليكم, "peace be upon you") and the farewell you learn last (مع السلامة (as-salāma) (maʿa s-salāma), "with safety") come from the same three consonants. Arabic opens and closes a conversation with one idea.

Two letters, both already yours, and a word that will carry the whole chapter.

blocks.title: You'll want to know — The letters

segments.text: (Skim if you read Arabic.) م (mīm) from Lesson 3 of the writing set, and ع (ʿayn) from Lesson 10 — the throat sound whose Phoenician ancestor meant "eye," and which the Greeks recycled into the vowel O.
Right to left: م, ع becomes maʿa. The ʿayn is not a vowel; it is a constriction deep in the throat. Take your time with it.

blocks.title: You'll want to know — The word

segments.text: مع (maʿa) = "with, together with."
It is a preposition, and unlike الـ (al-) or بـ (bi-) from Chapter 3, it is a free-standing word — it does not glue onto the next one. Compare:

utterances: الـ al- "the". attaches?: yes.
بـ bi- "in/with". attaches?: yes.
لـ li- "to". attaches?: yes.
مع maʿa "with". attaches?: no.

segments.text: So Arabic has two words touching on "with": the one-letter بـ (bi-, "in/by means of," as in bi-khayr) and the full word مع (maʿa, "accompanied by"). Bi-khayr is "in goodness"; maʿa is standing next to something.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way — The Semitic cousin

segments.text: maʿa from Semitic ʿimma, and its Hebrew cousin is עִם (ʿim), "with." The same pairing you met with salām / shalom in Chapter 1 and ism / shem in Chapter 2. Three chapters, three cousins — the family resemblance is systematic, not a coincidence.

the contrast — "bi-khayr in goodness, maʿa with"
the cousin — "maʿa, Hebrew ʿim"
مع (maʿa) — mīm joining into ʿayn

segments.text: What does مع mean? ("With.") Does it attach to the next word, like al- and bi-? (No — it stands alone.) What is the difference between bi- and maʿa? (Bi- = "in/by means of"; maʿa = "accompanied by".) What is its Hebrew cousin? (ʿim.) Next: the word it goes with — and you already know most of it.

lessons.title: السلامة (as-salāma) — "the safety"
lessons.gloss: the safety — Chapter 1's salām, plus a pattern and a feminine ending

segments.text: becomes السلامة (as-salāma) = al- + salām + -a = "the safety."
Every letter is one you have already written by hand.

blocks.title: You'll want to know — The pattern that changed the meaning

segments.text: Arabic doesn't just add endings — it pours a root into a shape. Here the root s–l–m goes into the pattern faʿāla, which turns a thing into the state of being that thing:

utterances: salām means peace.
salāma means safety, soundness, wellbeing — the state of being at peace.

segments.text: Same three consonants, one new shape, a new but related word. This is the engine Chapter 1 promised, working in front of you.

blocks.title: You'll want to know — Two small rules, both already learned

segments.text: 1. The sun letter. S (س) is a sun letter, so the l of al- assimilates to it: written الس, but said as-salāma, not al-salāma. The same thing happens in السلام عليكم — the greeting you have said since Chapter 1.
2. The feminine ة. Tāʾ marbūṭa marks salāma as feminine. Arabic abstract nouns very often are.

the pattern — "peace becomes the state of peace"

segments.text: مع (maʿa, "with") + السلامة (as-salāma, "the safety") becomes مع السلامة (maʿa s-salāma) — "with safety."
Said as one run: maʿa s-salāma — the a of maʿa swallows the al-'s vowel, and the sun-letter rule doubles the s.
It is not "goodbye" in the English sense of a plain sign-off. It is a wish: go in safety.

The family, one more time: salām (peace), salāma (safety), islām (submission, i.e. entering peace), muslim (one who does so).

blocks.title: You'll want to know — English does the same trick

segments.text: Goodbye looks like a single word. It is worn down from God be with ye. So the English farewell is also built on "with" — you are being commended to something protective as you go.

segments.text: Four languages, one instinct: as someone leaves, hand them over to safekeeping.

lessons.title: إلى اللقاء (ilā l-liqāʾ) — "see you"
lessons.gloss: see you — literally 'until the meeting', the structure Spanish borrowed a word for

segments.text: The other everyday farewell — and the one with a surprise waiting inside Spanish.

blocks.title: You'll want to know — A note on the letters

segments.text: (Skim if you read Arabic.) Two pieces here are beyond what the writing track has covered, so read them for now and draw them later:
ق (qāf) — a k made far back against the soft palate, deeper than ك (kāf). It is not in the letter set you have been writing from.

ى in إلى — this is alif maqṣūra, "shortened alif": it wears yāʾ's skeleton with no dots and is pronounced as a long ā. You already know from writing Lessons 4–5 that dots are what separate letters sharing a body; this is that same principle, taken one step further.
The rest — ا ل ء — you have written.

blocks.title: You'll want to know — The two pieces

utterances: إلى ilā means "to, until".
اللقاء al-liqāʾ means "the meeting".

segments.text: becomes إلى اللقاء (ilā l-liqāʾ) = "until the meeting."
لقاء (liqāʾ) comes from the root l–q–y, "to meet." The final ء is the hamza from writing Lesson 6 — a glottal stop, a real consonant here, not decoration.
Note ل is a sun letter too, so al-liqāʾ doubles the l, just as as-salāma doubled the s.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way — The Spanish surprise

segments.text: Spanish says goodbye like this:
hasta luego — "until later" hasta mañana — "until tomorrow".

Same shape as ilā l-liqāʾ: "until" + a future point. But it goes further — Spanish hasta is itself an Arabic loanword, from ḥattā ("until"). Of the roughly four thousand Arabic words Spanish took during the eight centuries of al-Andalus, most are nouns; hasta is one of the rare borrowed function words.
So Spanish did not merely copy the pattern — it borrowed the very word that builds it.

utterances: language: Arabic. farewell: ilā l-liqāʾ. shape: until + the meeting.
language: Spanish. farewell: hasta luego. shape: until ( from ḥattā) + later.
language: French. farewell: à bientôt. shape: to + soon.
language: Italian. farewell: a presto. shape: to + soon.
